meta.title: Time value of money: single sums and annuities
meta.summary: Why accountants need time value of money, simple and compound interest, future and present values of single sums, solving for rates and periods, and future and present values of ordinary annuities and annuities due.

videos.title: Why accountants need time value of money
videos.lecture: Lecture 6 · Time value of money I
videos.take: Many accounting measurements are present values: notes, bonds, leases, pensions and impairments

scenes.say: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar next year. In intermediate accounting, that idea is everywhere.

scenes.heading: Where present values appear
scenes.say: Present values measure notes with low or no stated interest, bonds, leases, pension obligations, impairment losses and many fair values. Master this lecture and the second half of the course is much easier.

scenes.heading: Simple vs compound interest
scenes.say: Simple interest is earned on the principal only: ten thousand dollars at eight percent for three years earns $2,400. Compound interest is earned on principal plus interest already earned: $2,597. Accounting uses compound interest.

sub: and the future or present value
scenes.say: Every problem has four variables: an amount, an interest rate per period, a number of periods, and a future or present value. Know three and you can find the fourth.
Match the rate to the period. Eight percent a year compounded quarterly means two percent per period, with four periods each year.

scenes.q: 12% a year compounded monthly for 2 years means:
scenes.say: Quick check. Twelve percent a year compounded monthly for two years means what rate and how many periods? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, one percent for twenty-four periods.

videos.title: Future value of a single sum
videos.lecture: Lecture 6 · Time value of money I

scenes.say: Bluestem puts $100,000 aside today to fund a new mold in five years. How much will it have?
The future value of a single sum is the present amount times one plus the interest rate, raised to the number of periods. Tables give the factor directly.

scenes.heading: Bluestem's fund at 6%
scenes.say: At six percent compounded annually for five years, the factor is one point three three eight two three. One hundred thousand dollars grows to $133,823.

scenes.heading: Year by year
scenes.say: Year by year, interest earns interest: $106,000, $112,360, and so on to $133,823. Compound interest adds $33,823, versus $30,000 with simple interest.
In a spreadsheet, the FV function gives the same answer. Enter the present value as a negative, because it's money going out.

scenes.q: $50,000 invested for 3 years at 10% compounded annually grows to:
scenes.say: Quick check. Fifty thousand dollars invested for three years at ten percent compounded annually grows to how much? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, $66,550: fifty thousand times one point three three one.

videos.title: Present value of a single sum
videos.lecture: Lecture 6 · Time value of money I
videos.take: PV = FV ÷ (1 + i)ⁿ: discounting is the reverse of compounding

scenes.say: Flip the question. Bluestem needs $500,000 in four years for a warehouse expansion. How much must it invest today?
The present value is the future amount divided by one plus the rate, raised to the number of periods. Discounting is just compounding in reverse.

scenes.heading: Warehouse fund at 5%
scenes.say: At five percent for four years, the present value factor is point eight two two seven. Bluestem must invest $411,351 today.
The higher the rate, or the longer the wait, the smaller the present value. At eight percent, Bluestem would need only $367,515 today.

Accounting use: if a dealer gives Bluestem a $500,000 note due in four years with no interest, the sale isn't really $500,000. At a five percent market rate, the revenue is $411,351, and the rest is interest earned over four years.

scenes.q: PV of $20,000 due in 2 years at 10%?
scenes.say: Quick check. What's the present value of twenty thousand dollars due in two years at ten percent? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, $16,529: twenty thousand divided by one point two one.

videos.title: Solving for the rate or the number of periods
videos.lecture: Lecture 6 · Time value of money I
videos.take: Rearrange the factor: factor = FV ÷ PV, then find the rate or periods in the table

scenes.say: Sometimes you know the amounts and need the rate or the time.

scenes.heading: What rate turns $200,000 into $300,000 in 6 years?
scenes.say: An investment of $200,000 grows to $300,000 in six years. The required future value factor is three hundred divided by two hundred, one point five. In the six-period row, seven percent gives one point five zero zero seven three. The rate is about seven percent.

scenes.heading: How long to double at 8%?
scenes.say: How long does money take to double at eight percent? Look for a factor of two in the eight percent column: nine periods gives one point nine nine nine.
A handy check is the rule of seventy-two: divide seventy-two by the rate. Seventy-two divided by eight is nine years.
In a spreadsheet, the RATE and NPER functions solve these exactly.

scenes.q: Using the rule of 72, how long does money take to double at 6%?
scenes.say: Quick check. Using the rule of seventy-two, how long does money take to double at six percent? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Future value of an annuity
videos.lecture: Lecture 6 · Time value of money I
videos.take: An annuity is equal payments at equal intervals; annuity due payments come at the start of each period

scenes.say: Instead of one deposit, Bluestem will put $50,000 into a fund every year for five years.

scenes.heading: Two kinds of annuity
scenes.say: An annuity is a series of equal payments at equal intervals. In an ordinary annuity, payments come at the end of each period, like loan payments. In an annuity due, they come at the start, like rent.

scenes.heading: Ordinary annuity: $50,000 a year, 5 years, 6%
scenes.say: For an ordinary annuity of $50,000 at the end of each year for five years at six percent, the factor is five point six three seven. The fund grows to $281,855: $250,000 deposited plus $31,855 of interest.

scenes.heading: Annuity due: deposits at the start
scenes.say: If Bluestem deposits at the start of each year, every payment earns one more period of interest. Multiply the ordinary factor by one point zero six: the fund grows to $298,766.
The best habit in this topic: draw a timeline and mark exactly when each payment falls before you pick a table.

scenes.q: Which is usually an annuity due?
scenes.say: Quick check. Which is usually an annuity due? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B: rent paid in advance.

videos.title: Present value of an annuity
videos.lecture: Lecture 6 · Time value of money I
videos.take: PV of an annuity values a stream of equal payments today; it measures loans, leases and bond interest

scenes.say: A supplier offers Bluestem a new paint line for five annual payments of $40,000. What does it really cost?

scenes.heading: Ordinary annuity: $40,000 a year, 5 years, 8%
scenes.say: At an eight percent market rate, the present value factor for five end-of-year payments is three point nine nine two seven. The cost today is $159,708, not $200,000.

scenes.heading: Recording the purchase
scenes.say: Bluestem records the equipment and the note at $159,708. The extra $40,292 it pays over five years is interest expense, recognized as time passes.

scenes.heading: If payments start today
scenes.say: If the first payment were due today, it's an annuity due. Multiply the factor by one point zero eight: the present value is $172,485. Earlier payments cost more in today's dollars.
In a spreadsheet, PV with the rate, periods and payment gives the ordinary annuity. Add a one as the type argument for an annuity due.

scenes.q: PV of $10,000 a year for 3 years at 10%, ordinary annuity (factor 2.48685)?
scenes.say: Quick check. What's the present value of ten thousand dollars a year for three years at ten percent, an ordinary annuity with factor two point four eight six eight five? Pause and pick.

warmup: Would you rather receive $100,000 today or $130,000 in five years? What does your answer depend on?
The interest rate (opportunity cost) and risk; sets up present value.
acts: Identify the rate per period and number of periods: (a) 10% compounded semiannually for 4 years; (b) 9% compounded quarterly for 3 years.
Bluestem deposits $75,000 today at 8% compounded annually. How much in 6 years? (factor 1.58687)
A dealer gives Bluestem a $90,000 non-interest-bearing note due in 3 years. Market rate 6% (factor 0.83962). How much revenue does Bluestem record now?
What rate makes $40,000 grow to $59,200 in 5 years? (FV factors, 5 periods: 7% 1.40255; 8% 1.46933)
Bluestem will deposit $20,000 at the end of each year for 10 years at 7% (FVA factor 13.81645). Fund balance? If deposits are at the start of each year?
A lease requires $25,000 at the start of each year for 4 years at 6% (PVA ordinary factor 3.46511). Present value?
case: Buy or lease the paint line

Bluestem can (A) pay $165,000 cash for the paint line today; (B) pay $40,000 at the end of each year for 5 years; or (C) pay $38,000 at the start of each year for 5 years. Bluestem can borrow at 8%. (PVA ordinary, 5 periods, 8% = 3.99271.)
Compute the present value of B.
Compute the present value of C.
How would Bluestem record option B on the balance sheet?
B: $159,708. C: 38,000 × 4.31213 = $163,861. A: $165,000. B is cheapest. Record equipment and a note payable at $159,708; interest expense recognized over 5 years.
exam: Explain the difference between an ordinary annuity and an annuity due, and show how to convert an ordinary annuity factor into an annuity due factor.
Payment timing at end vs beginning; multiply ordinary factor by (1 + i) for both FV and PV.
Bluestem must accumulate $600,000 in 8 years. It can earn 5% (FV of 1 factor 1.47746; FVA ordinary factor 9.54911). (a) Single deposit today? (b) Equal end-of-year deposits?
